finalReport.content:
> Worked example — fictional manuscript and illustrative review. No real study was evaluated and no AI call produced these findings.

## Overall Assessment
The experiment provides a useful comparison of two study packages, but it cannot isolate the effect of retrieval practice from extra time spent studying. The strongest next step is to narrow the claim and design a time-matched comparison.

## Preserved Strengths
Separate question pools and blinded scoring answer the concern about repeated test items. Preserve these details in the methods section. This supported defense applies to item familiarity, not to every aspect of the experiment.

## Priority Revisions
**1. Match the conclusion to the design.** Describe the result as an advantage for the combined intervention. The retrieval condition received thirty additional minutes of practice; the current study cannot separate retrieval from time on task.

**2. Make the next comparison decisive.** Use an active control with the same total study time to examine whether retrieval itself explains the advantage.

## Open Judgment Calls
The discussion acknowledges that transfer to other courses was not measured. Keep any broader recommendation tentative, and evaluate another course before claiming generalizability.

## Revision Plan
- Revise the abstract and discussion to refer to the combined intervention.
- Preserve the separate question-pool and blinded-scoring descriptions.
- Keep the single-course limitation beside the broader application claim.
- Plan a time-matched comparison and a replication in a second course.

## Finding Register
These three illustrative findings preserve the relationship between each concern, ruling, and source. Open **Findings & evidence** to read the full discussion.

### T1.E1 · Revision needed
Extra practice time confounds the reported advantage. **Source: pages 2 and 3.** The response concedes this limitation; the causal conclusion needs revision.

### T1.E2 · Supported
Separate practice and delayed-test question pools address the repeated-item concern. **Source: page 2.** The support is specific to that challenge.

### T1.E3 · Open question
Transfer beyond the tested course remains untested. **Source: page 3.** The limitation is disclosed; the appropriate strength of the broader recommendation remains a judgment call.

## Scope of This Review
One topic, three exchanges. Other aspects of the paper were not reviewed. These outcomes are not a score for the paper. Citation relevance and model confidence are not measures of scientific truth.

ILLUSTRATIVE MANUSCRIPT — created to explain Verdict. These are fictional study details, not published research.

Spaced retrieval and delayed recall

Abstract
We studied whether brief retrieval practice improves delayed recall in an introductory university course. Ninety-six students were randomly assigned to spaced retrieval or a rereading control. The retrieval group completed three additional ten-minute practice sessions over one week. Both groups completed a delayed test fourteen days after the lesson.

The retrieval group scored a mean of 67%, compared with 59% in the control group. We interpret this difference as evidence that spaced retrieval can improve learning.

1. Research question
Does adding spaced retrieval to ordinary study improve recall two weeks later? The intervention was evaluated within a single introductory course, using short-answer questions about the taught material.
